content.content:
1	# wal-store
2	
3	Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.
4	
5	## Requirements
6	
7	Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.
8	
9	## Install
10	
11	    python3 -m pip install -e .
12	
13	## Run
14	
15	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
16	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
17	    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>
18	
19	## Public interface
20	
21	`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
22	exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
23	line subcommand creates it).
24	- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
25	- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
26	- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
27	- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
28	  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
29	  the same call).
30	- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
31	  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
32	  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
33	  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
34	- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
35	- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
36	  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
37	  durable sequence.
38	- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
39	  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
40	- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
41	  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
42	  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
43	- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.
44	
45	## Scanning
46	
47	`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
48	returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
49	order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
50	exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
51	inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
52	unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
53	delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
54	only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
55	writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
56	invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
57	committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.
58	
59	The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
60	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
61	change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
62	sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
63	takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
64	of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
65	as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
66	context manager).
67	
68	## Resumable scans
69	
70	A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
71	the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
72	point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
73	token:
74	
75	- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
76	- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
77	  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
78	  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
79	  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.
80	
81	Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
82	the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
83	the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.
84	
85	The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
86	content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
87	scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
88	compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
89	writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
90	immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
91	never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
92	log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
93	be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
94	read-only store never publishes a snapshot copy when minting a token;
95	such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
96	reconstruct) that snapshot. The reader's only on-disk artifact is the
97	short-lived lease registered when its store or cursor opened, which keeps
98	that snapshot in use across processes for as long as the resumed scan is
99	alive.
100	
101	Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
102	resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
103	later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
104	neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
105	snapshot after the delete never shows the key.
106	
107	A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
108	corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
109	reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
110	foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
111	`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
112	`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
113	coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
114	the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
115	(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
116	be handed across platforms and processes.
117	
118	
119	## Historical snapshot lifecycle
120	
121	Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
122	without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
123	minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
124	every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
125	so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):
126	
127	- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
128	  one merely iterating, with no token minted), any live read-only store or
129	  any resumed scan is serving that snapshot, in this process or in *any
130	  other process*. Cross-process users register a short-lived lease sidecar
131	  (`wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>`, the only kind of file a reader ever writes):
132	  it lists the snapshots that process has in use with a heartbeat, and the
133	  writer reads every lease before removing a copy (re-reading them
134	  immediately before each unlink, so a lease taken mid-sweep still
135	  protects its copy). Cursors and resume sessions register leases on
136	  either open form of the store — a writer's cursor or resumed scan
137	  registers with exactly the same scope as a read-only one. An orderly
138	  close removes the lease; a process killed without closing stops
139	  heartbeating, and expiry is then detected two ways — the heartbeat goes
140	  stale after the lease TTL, and a lease whose owning process no longer
141	  exists expires immediately — after which the lease pins nothing and is
142	  swept. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
143	  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
144	  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
145	  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
146	  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
147	- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
148	  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
149	- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
150	  (no in-process pin and no fresh lease in any process) are deleted.
151	
152	Every use of a copy also verifies it against the content identity in its
153	name: when the store is opened, when a token is resumed, and when the
154	writer decides during reclamation whether a copy is usable, the bytes on
155	disk must hash to that identity. A copy whose content does not match is
156	damaged: it is never trusted as a source, never guessed at and never
157	repaired in place, and it changes neither the committed state nor any
158	read by a byte. Reads and resumed scans rebuild the snapshot from the
159	committed log prefix or the checkpoint instead — byte-for-byte the result
160	a healthy copy would have served — and the writer reclaims the damaged
161	file in its ordinary sweep (a damaged copy of the *current* snapshot is
162	atomically replaced with the authoritative image on the next publish).
163	Publishing and replacing copies stays atomic and kill-safe, so a kill at
164	any point and a reopen converge to the same copy set.
165	
166	A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
167	keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
168	committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A damaged copy (its content
169	failing the identity in its name) counts as no copy at all — it is never
170	read from and is reclaimed by the writer. Only once every copy is gone
171	or damaged and neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can
172	rebuild the snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
173	truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
174	`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.
175	
176	Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
177	a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
178	next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete a
179	usable in-use copy (one named by an in-process pin or by any fresh
180	lease — a damaged copy serves no one and is removed regardless),
181	cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state, and never
182	touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only dead or
183	damaged
184	`wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies and, once expired, stale `wal.lease.*`
185	sidecars. Each lease sidecar is written only by its owner and is
186	atomically replaced (never edited in place), so registering, expiring
187	and reclaiming converge after a kill in any process to one in-use set
188	and one copy set. It adds no command-line subcommand: everything lives
189	in the same store directory behind the existing `scan`/token calls, and
190	the lease is the one kind of new file — a reader writes nothing else.
191	
192	
193	## Range deletes
194	
195	`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
196	of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
197	bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
198	`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
199	the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
200	shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
201	removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
202	endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
203	`ValueError`.
204	
205	Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
206	it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
207	writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
208	committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
209	alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
210	back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
211	new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
212	with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.
213	
214	Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
215	report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
216	it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
217	contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
218	reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
219	scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.
220	
221	## Read-only stores
222	
223	`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
224	number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
225	same directory. A reader takes no lock and never touches the log, a
226	checkpoint or a snapshot copy; the only file it creates is its own
227	short-lived lease sidecar, registering the snapshots it has in use so a
228	writer in another process keeps them (best-effort — a read-only
229	directory simply has no lease, and the lease is removed again on close
230	or expires by heartbeat if the process is killed). It pins a snapshot at
231	open time and every `get` reads from that one complete committed
232	snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written commit, a torn record
233	or a half-finished shrink are never visible. Successive reads from the
234	same reader may advance across snapshots only by reopening; each read is
235	of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not replay the log and do not
236	block the writer: killing or suspending a reader never affects the
237	writer's commits, recovery or stats (a killed reader leaves only a lease
238	that is ignored once stale and then swept). `put`, `delete`, `commit`
239	and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports the
240	pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
241	from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
242	prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.
243	
244	`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
245	it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
246	replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
247	leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
248	which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
249	`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.
250	
251	## Recovery
252	
253	`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:
254	
255	- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
256	- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
257	  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
258	- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.
259	
260	A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
261	recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
262	to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
263	tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
264	reopened.
265	
266	### Recovery may itself be killed
267	
268	Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
269	point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
270	and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
271	of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
272	regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.
273	
274	Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are
275	not part of the public API and are maintained entirely below the write
276	path:
277	
278	- `wal.ckp` is an atomically replaced copy of the log prefix ending at the
279	  most recent commit marker. A log torn at *any* offset — even offset 0, or
280	  inside the committed prefix — is silently rebuilt from it, so a
281	  half-finished convergence can never be mistaken for a torn tail or for
282	  corruption.
283	- `wal.rec` is a small marker written after validation and before the
284	  repair, recording the clean prefix length and the discarded count. A
285	  repair interrupted mid-copy is simply repeated on reopen, and the marker
286	  keeps `discarded` stable across reopens and repeated recoveries until the
287	  next successful commit closes the epoch.
288	
289	Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,
290	a length out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
291	sequence is corruption: recovery raises `wal_store.CorruptLogError`
292	(a subclass of `ValueError`) and stops without applying or removing
293	anything.
294	
295	The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with
296	the same key order and a trailing newline, e.g.
297	`{"applied":2,"discarded":0,"seq":1}`. Discarding a torn tail is not an
298	error and the exit code is `0`; corruption prints one explanatory line to
299	standard error and exits `3` without printing the JSON line.
300	
301	## Compaction
302	
303	`compact()` reclaims history without sacrificing any committed state. When
304	it finishes, the log contains exactly the live committed key/values: one
305	put frame per currently committed key, in sorted key order, followed by a
306	base commit marker that carries the pre-compaction sequence. Deleted keys
307	are gone for good — a deleted key can never reappear — and overwritten keys
308	keep only their final value. The durable sequence number is unchanged, so
309	the next `commit()` writes `seq + 1`; every commit advances, including an
310	empty one, and subsequent commits continue the strict sequence as if no
311	rewrite had happened. The empty committed state
312	(including "everything was deleted") compacts to an empty log.
313	
314	`compact()` returns the same three-field report shape as `recover()`:
315	`applied` is the number of live puts the new log contains, `discarded` is
316	always `0` and `seq` is the preserved sequence. Uncommitted session changes
317	make it raise `ValueError`; commit or discard them first.
318	
319	Compaction is a kill-safe, idempotent convergence like recovery. The new
320	image is assembled in memory and durably staged as the `wal.cmp` sidecar
321	(an atomically replaced complete file, never an in-place edit), then
322	published in two atomic steps — `wal.ckp` first and `wal.log` second —
323	before the staging file is removed. A process killed at any point, any
324	number of times, leaves a store that finishes the identical publish on the
325	next open: the recovered state is exactly the last committed state, the
326	sequence never regresses and the resulting log/sidecar bytes are
327	byte-identical to one uninterrupted compaction. Repeating compaction on an
328	already compact store produces the same bytes.
329	
330	Live read-only stores are unaffected: they keep serving the complete
331	snapshot they pinned before, during and after compaction (it lands on the

# wal-store

Key value store that appends every mutation to a write-ahead log first, so a process killed between writes and checkpoints recovers exactly the committed state.

## Requirements

Python 3.11 or newer. Standard library only.

## Install

    python3 -m pip install -e .

## Run

    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store recover
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store put <key> --value-file <path>
    python3 -m wal_store --path ./store get <key>

## Public interface

`wal_store.Store(path)` opens the store directory. The directory must
exist; opening a missing path raises `FileNotFoundError` (the `put` command
line subcommand creates it).
- `put(key, value) -> None` records a mutation.
- `get(key) -> bytes | None` reads the value at the last committed snapshot.
- `delete(key) -> None` records a removal.
- `delete_range(start=None, end=None) -> None` records a batch removal of
  every committed key in a half-open byte range (`delete(start, end)` is
  the same call).
- `commit() -> int` advances the durable sequence number. Every call writes
  a commit marker and advances the sequence by exactly one, including a
  commit with no pending changes; the first commit after a compaction is the
  pre-compaction sequence plus one.
- `recover() -> dict` replays the log and reports what it applied.
- `compact() -> dict` rewrites committed history into one tight log and
  reclaims the old space, without changing the committed state or the
  durable sequence.
- `scan(start=None, end=None) -> ScanCursor` opens an ordered read-only
  cursor over the committed snapshot pinned at that moment.
- `ScanCursor.token() -> bytes` (alias `mark()`) serialises the cursor's
  current position into a resumable scan token; `scan(token=tok)`
  (alias `scan(resume=tok)`) continues that scan from the token.
- `stats() -> dict` reports sequence, entries and bytes.

## Scanning

`scan()` works on both open forms and never touches the write path. The
returned cursor is an iterator of `(key, value)` pairs in bytewise key
order — keys compare by their raw UTF-8 bytes and values come back as the
exact stored bytes, with no encoding conversion — covering `start`
inclusive through `end` exclusive; a `None` endpoint leaves that side
unbounded, so `scan()` walks everything. Keys that only ever appeared in
delete records never show up, a key overwritten any number of times yields
only its last committed value, and empty values scan like any other. A
writer's uncommitted changes are not part of the snapshot — they are
invisible to `scan()` and to `get()` alike, both of which read the last
committed snapshot; a read-only store scans the snapshot it pinned at open.

The snapshot is materialised once when the cursor opens, so later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space never
change what the cursor yields, and the same snapshot scans to the identical
sequence before and after compaction. Scanning never replays the log,
takes no lock and keeps no history in memory, so its cost is independent
of the log's length. A `start` that sorts after `end` raises `ValueError`,
as does reading from a cursor after `close()` (the cursor is also a
context manager).

## Resumable scans

A scan can be paused and later continued from exactly where it stopped, in
the same process or after reopening the store (writer or read-only). At any
point a cursor can serialise its current position into an opaque `bytes`
token:

- `ScanCursor.token()` returns the token; `mark()` is an alias.
- `Store.scan(token=tok)` opens a new cursor that continues the identical
  range from the identical position over the identical snapshot;
  `scan(resume=tok)` is an alias. The token already carries its range, so
  passing `start`/`end` together with a token raises `ValueError`.

Splitting one scan at a token and concatenating the pieces yields exactly
the pairs a single uninterrupted scan would have yielded, byte for byte:
the resumed stream is the tail of the original scan.

The token names the snapshot it pins — the durable sequence number and a
content identity over the snapshot's canonical image — together with the
scan range and the next position. It stays valid across later commits,
compaction, crash recovery and reclamation of the old log space. When a
writer mints a token it durably publishes the pinned snapshot as an
immutable, content-addressed `wal.s<seq>.<id>` sidecar (an atomic write,
never edited in place), so the token keeps resolving after the underlying
log bytes are compacted away; snapshots that were never published can also
be reconstructed from the committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A
read-only store never publishes a snapshot copy when minting a token;
such a token still resolves because the writer has published (or can
reconstruct) that snapshot. The reader's only on-disk artifact is the
short-lived lease registered when its store or cursor opened, which keeps
that snapshot in use across processes for as long as the resumed scan is
alive.

Deleted keys never come back. A token pins one exact committed snapshot:
resuming it reads precisely that snapshot, whether or not the same keys were
later deleted, and a range tombstone that compaction has since reclaimed
neither removes nor revives anything on the resumed path. A fresh scan of a
snapshot after the delete never shows the key.

A token is opaque and strictly validated. Anything forged, truncated,
corrupted (checksum mismatch), carrying an out-of-range position, naming a
reversed range, or referring to a snapshot this store does not hold (a
foreign store, or a snapshot whose every copy has been reclaimed) raises
`ValueError`; nothing is guessed or repaired. A non-`bytes` token raises
`TypeError` — `bytearray` and `memoryview` are not accepted and are never
coerced. The token format is platform-independent: the same snapshot at
the same position always mints byte-identical tokens on Windows and Linux
(all integers are big-endian and no bytes are translated), so tokens can
be handed across platforms and processes.


## Historical snapshot lifecycle

Minting a token publishes one immutable `wal.s<seq>.<id>` snapshot copy;
without lifecycle management those copies pile up forever, one per
minted snapshot. Reclamation fixes which copies survive and runs after
every commit and every compaction (and is finished at every writer open,
so a sweep killed mid-run simply completes on reopen):

- **In use** — a copy is never reclaimed while any open cursor (including
  one merely iterating, with no token minted), any live read-only store or
  any resumed scan is serving that snapshot, in this process or in *any
  other process*. Cross-process users register a short-lived lease sidecar
  (`wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>`, the only kind of file a reader ever writes):
  it lists the snapshots that process has in use with a heartbeat, and the
  writer reads every lease before removing a copy (re-reading them
  immediately before each unlink, so a lease taken mid-sweep still
  protects its copy). Cursors and resume sessions register leases on
  either open form of the store — a writer's cursor or resumed scan
  registers with exactly the same scope as a read-only one. An orderly
  close removes the lease; a process killed without closing stops
  heartbeating, and expiry is then detected two ways — the heartbeat goes
  stale after the lease TTL, and a lease whose owning process no longer
  exists expires immediately — after which the lease pins nothing and is
  swept. An in-use token keeps pointing at the same
  snapshot across commits, compactions and crash recovery; resuming it is
  byte-for-byte the tail of the original one-shot scan. Reclamation
  deletes only redundant copies — the reads and resumes in flight do not
  change by a byte, and a deleted key never comes back.
- **Always retained** — the current committed snapshot and the newest
  three published predecessor generations are never reclaimed.
- **Everything else** — copies outside the retention window with no user
  (no in-process pin and no fresh lease in any process) are deleted.

Every use of a copy also verifies it against the content identity in its
name: when the store is opened, when a token is resumed, and when the
writer decides during reclamation whether a copy is usable, the bytes on
disk must hash to that identity. A copy whose content does not match is
damaged: it is never trusted as a source, never guessed at and never
repaired in place, and it changes neither the committed state nor any
read by a byte. Reads and resumed scans rebuild the snapshot from the
committed log prefix or the checkpoint instead — byte-for-byte the result
a healthy copy would have served — and the writer reclaims the damaged
file in its ordinary sweep (a damaged copy of the *current* snapshot is
atomically replaced with the authoritative image on the next publish).
Publishing and replacing copies stays atomic and kill-safe, so a kill at
any point and a reopen converge to the same copy set.

A copy disappearing does not by itself invalidate a token: the token
keeps working for as long as that snapshot can still be rebuilt from the
committed log prefix or the checkpoint. A damaged copy (its content
failing the identity in its name) counts as no copy at all — it is never
read from and is reclaimed by the writer. Only once every copy is gone
or damaged and neither the surviving log prefix nor the checkpoint can
rebuild the snapshot does resuming an old token raise `ValueError`. Forged,
truncated, corrupted, out-of-range or cross-snapshot tokens raise
`ValueError` just as before; the store never guesses or repairs them.

Reclamation is an idempotent convergence: independent file unlinks with
a directory sync at the end, so a kill at any point leaves a state the
next open converges to the identical file set. It cannot delete a
usable in-use copy (one named by an in-process pin or by any fresh
lease — a damaged copy serves no one and is removed regardless),
cannot move the durable sequence or the committed state, and never
touches `wal.log`, `wal.ckp` or any record; it removes only dead or
damaged
`wal.s<seq>.<id>` copies and, once expired, stale `wal.lease.*`
sidecars. Each lease sidecar is written only by its owner and is
atomically replaced (never edited in place), so registering, expiring
and reclaiming converge after a kill in any process to one in-use set
and one copy set. It adds no command-line subcommand: everything lives
in the same store directory behind the existing `scan`/token calls, and
the lease is the one kind of new file — a reader writes nothing else.


## Range deletes

`delete_range(start=None, end=None)` removes every committed key a scan
of the same endpoints would return: keys compare by their raw UTF-8
bytes, the range is half-open (`start` inclusive, `end` exclusive) and a
`None` endpoint leaves that side unbounded, so `delete_range()` clears
the whole store while `delete_range("a", "a")` removes nothing. The
shorthand `delete(start, end)` is the same call; `delete(key)` still
removes one key. Endpoint validation is shared with `scan`: non-string
endpoints raise `TypeError` and a `start` sorting after `end` raises
`ValueError`.

Like every other mutation the tombstone is only staged in the session:
it is invisible to scans and read-only stores until `commit()`, and a
writer that is killed first reopens at the last committed state. Once
committed, the covered keys disappear from single-key reads and scans
alike, and a key that only ever appears in delete history can never come
back. Writing a key inside a previously deleted range simply stores the
new value — after commit it reads back as that last committed value,
with keys and values still handled as raw bytes.

Recovery resolves a range tombstone by removing the covered keys; the
report counts the tombstone record under `applied`. Compaction reclaims
it together with the rest of the dead history: the compacted image
contains one live put per surviving key and no tombstones at all, so
reclaiming the record can never resurrect a deleted key, and a snapshot
scans to the identical bytes before and after compaction.

## Read-only stores

`wal_store.Store(path, read_only=True)` opens an isolated reader. Any
number of read-only processes may coexist with the single writer in the
same directory. A reader takes no lock and never touches the log, a
checkpoint or a snapshot copy; the only file it creates is its own
short-lived lease sidecar, registering the snapshots it has in use so a
writer in another process keeps them (best-effort — a read-only
directory simply has no lease, and the lease is removed again on close
or expires by heartbeat if the process is killed). It pins a snapshot at
open time and every `get` reads from that one complete committed
snapshot, so uncommitted mutations, a half-written commit, a torn record
or a half-finished shrink are never visible. Successive reads from the
same reader may advance across snapshots only by reopening; each read is
of one fully committed snapshot. Reads do not replay the log and do not
block the writer: killing or suspending a reader never affects the
writer's commits, recovery or stats (a killed reader leaves only a lease
that is ignored once stale and then swept). `put`, `delete`, `commit`
and `recover` are rejected on a read-only store; `stats` reports the
pinned snapshot and `get` is the normal way to read it. Readers serve
from the atomically replaced `wal.ckp` sidecar (and the committed log
prefix), so directories written by older versions open directly.

`wal_store.inject_tear(source, destination, offset)` is a verification aid:
it writes a byte-for-byte copy of `source` cut at exactly `offset` bytes (a
replica of a process killed at that write position) to `destination` and
leaves the source untouched. Either argument may be a store directory, in
which case its `wal.log` is used. A negative or past-the-end offset raises
`IndexError`. It is never used by the normal write path.

## Recovery

`recover()` returns a report with three integer fields, in this key order:

- `applied` — committed put/delete records replayed into the state,
- `discarded` — torn tail records dropped (at most one, the unfinished final
  write left by a process killed mid append; `0` on a clean log),
- `seq` — the durable sequence number after recovery.

A record killed halfway through is not a mutation: it is discarded and the
recovered state is exactly the last committed state. An empty log recovers
to an empty state, which is a normal result. Recovery truncates the dirty
tail and the next commit uses `seq + 1`, no matter how often the store is
reopened.

### Recovery may itself be killed

Recovery is an idempotent, kill-safe convergence. Interrupting it at any
point — while the dirty tail is being dropped or the log is being rebuilt —
and reopening any number of times reaches exactly the state and the report
of one clean recovery, with exit code `0`; the durable sequence never
regresses and the next commit is always `seq + 1`.

Two internal sidecar files in the store directory make this work; they are
not part of the public API and are maintained entirely below the write
path:

- `wal.ckp` is an atomically replaced copy of the log prefix ending at the
  most recent commit marker. A log torn at *any* offset — even offset 0, or
  inside the committed prefix — is silently rebuilt from it, so a
  half-finished convergence can never be mistaken for a torn tail or for
  corruption.
- `wal.rec` is a small marker written after validation and before the
  repair, recording the clean prefix length and the discarded count. A
  repair interrupted mid-copy is simply repeated on reopen, and the marker
  keeps `discarded` stable across reopens and repeated recoveries until the
  next successful commit closes the epoch.

Only the final record may be incomplete. Any incomplete record elsewhere,
a length out of bounds, unparseable content, or a duplicate/regressing
sequence is corruption: recovery raises `wal_store.CorruptLogError`
(a subclass of `ValueError`) and stops without applying or removing
anything.

The command line `recover` prints the report as one compact JSON line with
the same key order and a trailing newline, e.g.
`{"applied":2,"discarded":0,"seq":1}`. Discarding a torn tail is not an
error and the exit code is `0`; corruption prints one explanatory line to
standard error and exits `3` without printing the JSON line.

## Compaction

`compact()` reclaims history without sacrificing any committed state. When
it finishes, the log contains exactly the live committed key/values: one
put frame per currently committed key, in sorted key order, followed by a
base commit marker that carries the pre-compaction sequence. Deleted keys
are gone for good — a deleted key can never reappear — and overwritten keys
keep only their final value. The durable sequence number is unchanged, so
the next `commit()` writes `seq + 1`; every commit advances, including an
empty one, and subsequent commits continue the strict sequence as if no
rewrite had happened. The empty committed state
(including "everything was deleted") compacts to an empty log.

`compact()` returns the same three-field report shape as `recover()`:
`applied` is the number of live puts the new log contains, `discarded` is
always `0` and `seq` is the preserved sequence. Uncommitted session changes
make it raise `ValueError`; commit or discard them first.

Compaction is a kill-safe, idempotent convergence like recovery. The new
image is assembled in memory and durably staged as the `wal.cmp` sidecar
(an atomically replaced complete file, never an in-place edit), then
published in two atomic steps — `wal.ckp` first and `wal.log` second —
before the staging file is removed. A process killed at any point, any
number of times, leaves a store that finishes the identical publish on the
next open: the recovered state is exactly the last committed state, the
sequence never regresses and the resulting log/sidecar bytes are
byte-identical to one uninterrupted compaction. Repeating compaction on an
already compact store produces the same bytes.

Live read-only stores are unaffected: they keep serving the complete
snapshot they pinned before, during and after compaction (it lands on the
other half of the same log-versus-checkpoint pair readers already choose
between), while fresh readers open the compacted snapshot. No reader ever
sees a mix of old and new bytes, a half-written file, or content whose
space was reclaimed; killing a reader does not disturb compaction and
killing the compactor does not disturb a reader. Compaction introduces no
new limits beyond the existing single-writer rule, and directories written
by older versions compact directly with no conversion step.

## Tests

    python3 -m unittest discover -s tests -t .

## Limits

One writer at a time; no cross-process locking.
Values are bytes; encoding is the caller concern.
No replication; compaction is a writer-initiated rewrite, not background
garbage collection.

153	Read-only processes (``Store(path, read_only=True)``) take no lock and never
154	touch the log, the checkpoint or any snapshot copy: the only file a reader
155	creates is its own short-lived lease sidecar (best-effort, and absent
156	altogether in a read-only directory). At open each one picks the highest
157	committed prefix available at that instant -- the validated ``wal.log``
158	prefix or ``wal.ckp`` -- scans it once into memory and serves every ``get``
159	from that index. Because the chosen image is complete and is only ever
160	replaced atomically (never edited in place), a refresh caught mid-rename, a
161	half-written commit, a torn record, or a log being rebuilt, shrunk or
162	compacted can never expose partial bytes: each read lands on one full
163	committed snapshot that was current at or after the open. A directory
164	written by an older version is opened the same way from its log and
165	checkpoint. Reads never replay the log afterwards, so their cost is
166	independent of history and they never block the writer; a reader that hangs
167	changes no data, and one that is killed merely leaves a lease that expires
168	by heartbeat and is swept, never affecting the committed state.
169	
170	Compaction (``Store.compact()``) rewrites the committed history into one
171	tight image without losing a byte of committed state. The compacted log
172	holds exactly the live puts -- one per currently committed key, in sorted
173	key order -- followed by a *base commit* marker carrying the pre-compaction
174	sequence number. The durable sequence keeps that value, so the next commit
175	is ``seq + 1`` and every later commit continues the strict sequence; keys
176	that were deleted never come back. The image is assembled in memory and
177	staged as the atomically replaced ``wal.cmp`` sidecar; finishing installs
178	it as ``wal.ckp`` first and as ``wal.log`` second. Every intermediate state
179	is therefore either the pair of old files or the pair of complete new
180	images, which is precisely the two-image world the reader already chooses
181	between: a kill anywhere leaves a state reopening converges by simply
182	repeating the finish, and interrupting compaction any number of times
183	produces the same bytes as one clean run. Live readers keep serving their
184	pinned old snapshots (the inode survives on Unix; on Windows readers hold
185	no writer-side fd) and new readers land on the new snapshot, never a mix,
186	a half-written file or a byte that was already reclaimed.
187	
188	The durable commit boundary is the highest of the validated log boundary,
189	the checkpoint boundary and the marker boundary, so it can never move
190	backwards. Every repair step is either idempotent or an atomic rename; a
191	kill between any two steps leaves a state the next open converges from to
192	the identical result.
193	
194	Log frame layout (all integers big-endian)::
195	
196	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
197	    | b"WAL2" | payload_length | header_crc | payload              | crc32   |
198	    | 4 bytes | 8 bytes        | 4 bytes    | metadata\\n<value>    | 4 bytes |
199	    +---------+----------------+------------+----------------------+---------+
200	
201	``header_crc`` is the crc32 of the magic and length bytes. It makes a
202	partial header that borrows bytes from a following frame fail validation,
203	so an incomplete record in the middle of the log reads as corruption while
204	a genuinely short final header reads as a torn tail.
205	
206	Metadata is a compact JSON object: ``{"t":"p","k":key}`` for puts,
207	``{"t":"d","k":key}`` for deletes, ``{"t":"r","s":start,"e":end}`` for
208	range tombstones (``null`` marks an unbounded side), ``{"t":"c","s":seq}``
209	for ordinary commits and ``{"t":"b","s":seq}`` for the base commit that
210	closes a compacted log. The two carry the sequence identically; a base
211	marker is additionally required to be the first commit marker in its file.
212	The raw value bytes follow the first newline, so values need no encoding.
213	
214	A range tombstone covers every committed key whose raw UTF-8 bytes sort at
215	or after its start and strictly before its end (half-open). It is resolved
216	when the log is replayed -- matching keys are popped then -- and, like an
217	ordinary delete frame, carries no state of its own. Compaction therefore
218	reclaims it together with every other dead record: the live puts the
219	compact image contains already exclude each deleted key, so dropping the
220	tombstone can never make one reappear.
221	"""

241	class CorruptLogError(ValueError):
242	    """The write-ahead log is corrupt, not merely missing a torn tail.
243	
244	    A single incomplete final record is a normal crash remnant and is
245	    discarded during recovery. Anything else that fails framing, checksum,
246	    metadata or commit-sequence validation is corruption; recovery stops
247	    without applying or removing anything.

251	class ScanCursor:
252	    """Ordered read-only cursor over one pinned committed snapshot.
253	
254	    Created by :meth:`Store.scan`. Iterating yields ``(key, value)`` pairs
255	    in bytewise key order -- keys ordered by their raw UTF-8 bytes, values
256	    returned as the exact stored bytes -- covering the range given at open:
257	    the start key inclusive, the end key exclusive, either side unbounded
258	    when its endpoint was ``None``.
259	
260	    The snapshot is fully materialised when the cursor opens, so later
261	    commits, compaction, crash recovery or reclamation of the old log space
262	    never change what the cursor yields, and closing the store it came from
263	    does not disturb it. The cursor is an iterator; it is also a context
264	    manager, and ``close()`` releases the snapshot early. Reading from a
265	    closed cursor raises ``ValueError``.
266	
267	    :meth:`token` serialises the current position into an opaque ``bytes``
268	    token naming the pinned snapshot, the scan range and the next position.
269	    ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this process or in a freshly opened
270	    store -- continues the identical scan from that position.
271	    """
272	
273	    def __init__(self, items, lo_idx=0, hi_idx=None, pos=None, seq=0,
274	                 lo=None, hi=None, publisher=None, sid=None, leases=None):
275	        # ``items`` is the materialised snapshot: (key, value) pairs already
276	        # sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. The visible window is
277	        # [lo_idx, hi_idx) and the next position starts at ``pos``.
278	        self._items = items
279	        self._lo_idx = lo_idx
280	        self._hi_idx = len(items) if hi_idx is None else hi_idx
281	        self._pos = lo_idx if pos is None else pos
282	        self._seq = seq
283	        self._lo = lo
284	        self._hi = hi
285	        # Writer-only callback durably publishing the pinned snapshot so a
286	        # minted token survives compaction and reclamation; ``None`` on
287	        # read-only stores, which never create or modify any file.
288	        self._publisher = publisher
289	        self._sid = sid
290	        # An open cursor counts as a user of its snapshot for the
291	        # reclamation rules: its box keeps the snapshot's pin alive in the
292	        # process-wide pin set until ``close()`` (or destruction), so
293	        # reclamation never removes the copy an open cursor is over. The
294	        # content identity is derived lazily on the first token mint, or at
295	        # open when a cross-process lease must be registered with it.
296	        self._box = _register_snapshot(seq, items, sid)
297	        # Every cursor -- opened on a read-only store or on a writer --
298	        # additionally holds a cross-process lease for its pinned snapshot
299	        # (``leases`` is the opening store's lease registry), so a writer in
300	        # *another* process treats the snapshot as in use even after this
301	        # cursor's own store has closed. A read-only cursor's identity is
302	        # already known from the store's open; a writer cursor's is derived
303	        # here, at open, so its registration scope matches a reader's.
304	        self._leases = leases
305	        self._lease_held = False
306	        self._lease_finalizer = None
307	        # Only a snapshot that actually has a published copy (seq >= 1) can
308	        # need cross-process protection.
309	        if leases is not None and seq >= 1:
310	            if sid is None:
311	                # The pin box owns the identity derivation and its lazy
312	                # cache; the cursor only reads the identity back and never
313	                # writes the box's fields.
314	                sid = self._box.sid()
315	                self._sid = sid
316	            leases.acquire(seq, sid)
317	            self._lease_held = True
318	            # A cursor dropped without close() must release its lease the way
319	            # its weak in-process pin releases on GC.
320	            self._lease_finalizer = weakref.finalize(
321	                self, _release_lease, leases, seq, sid)
322	        self._closed = False
323	
324	    def __iter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
325	        return self
326	
327	    def __next__(self):
328	        if self._closed:
329	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
330	        if self._pos >= self._hi_idx:
331	            raise StopIteration
332	        item = self._items[self._pos]
333	        self._pos += 1
334	        return item
335	
336	    def token(self) -> bytes:
337	        """Serialise the current position into an opaque scan token.
338	
339	        The returned ``bytes`` name the pinned snapshot (its durable
340	        sequence number and content identity), the scan range and the next
341	        position. Feeding the token to ``Store.scan(token=...)`` -- in this
342	        process or in a freshly opened store, writer or read-only -- opens
343	        a cursor that continues the same range from the same position over
344	        the same pinned snapshot, byte-identical to the tail of this scan.
345	
346	        Token bytes are platform-independent and deterministic: the same
347	        snapshot at the same position always mints the same token. On a
348	        writer store minting also publishes the pinned snapshot as an
349	        immutable sidecar so the token survives compaction and reclamation
350	        of the old log space; a read-only store never publishes a snapshot
351	        copy when minting (it only holds the cross-process lease registered
352	        when the cursor opened).
353	        """
354	        if self._closed:
355	            raise ValueError("scan cursor is closed")
356	        if self._sid is None:
357	            # The pin box derives and caches the identity, so the in-use
358	            # check at reclamation never hashes this snapshot again either.
359	            self._sid = self._box.sid()
360	        if self._publisher is not None:
361	            self._publisher(self._seq, self._sid, self._items)
362	        return _encode_token(self._seq, self._sid, self._lo, self._hi,
363	                             self._pos)
364	
365	    def mark(self) -> bytes:
366	        """Alias for :meth:`token`."""
367	        return self.token()
368	
369	    @property
370	    def closed(self) -> bool:
371	        return self._closed
372	
373	    def close(self) -> None:
374	        if self._closed:
375	            return
376	        _unpin_snapshot(self._box)
377	        if self._lease_held:
378	            # Detach the GC finalizer: this explicit release is the one.
379	            if self._lease_finalizer is not None:
380	                self._lease_finalizer.detach()
381	            self._leases.release(self._seq, self._sid)
382	            self._lease_held = False
383	        self._items = []
384	        self._box = None
385	        self._closed = True
386	
387	    def __enter__(self) -> "ScanCursor":
388	        return self
389	
390	    def __exit__(self, exc_type, exc, tb) -> None:
391	        self.close()

395	_CHECKPOINT_NAME = "wal.ckp"
396	_MARKER_NAME = "wal.rec"
397	_COMPACT_NAME = "wal.cmp"

399	_MAGIC = b"WAL2"
400	_PREFIX = 12  # 4 bytes magic + 8 bytes payload length
401	_HEADER = 16   # prefix + 4 bytes crc32 of the prefix
402	_TRAILER = 4   # crc32 of the payload
403	_MAX_PAYLOAD = 1 << 40

405	_OP_PUT = "p"
406	_OP_DELETE = "d"
407	_OP_RANGE = "r"
408	_OP_COMMIT = "c"
409	_OP_BASE = "b"
410	_COMMIT_OPS = (_OP_COMMIT, _OP_BASE)

413	# Pinned-snapshot sidecars (``wal.s<seq>.<id>``) and scan tokens. A token
414	# is an opaque, platform-independent byte string: magic, the snapshot's
415	# durable sequence, its 32-byte content identity, the optional range
416	# endpoints, the next position and a checksum -- all integers big-endian,
417	# so the same snapshot and position mint byte-identical tokens everywhere.
418	_TOKEN_MAGIC = b"WST1"

422	# many published snapshot copies are always retained; older copies are
423	# reclaimed once nothing is using them.
424	_SNAPSHOT_RETENTION = 3

426	# Cross-process in-use registration. The in-process pin set only names users
427	# in the opening process, so a snapshot pinned by a cursor or a read-only
428	# store in *another* process would look free to this writer's reclamation.
429	# Each lease-holding process therefore owns one short-lived sidecar of the
430	# single ``wal.lease.*`` kind: it lists the snapshots that process has in use
431	# together with a heartbeat timestamp, and is atomically rewritten in place.
432	# The writer reads every lease sidecar before removing a copy and treats
433	# every fresh one as an in-use pin. An orderly close removes the file; a
434	# process killed without closing stops heartbeating, so once its timestamp
435	# is older than the TTL it pins nothing and its stale sidecar is swept.
436	_LEASE_PREFIX = "wal.lease."
437	_LEASE_REC_PREFIX = "wal.l"
438	_LEASE_HEARTBEAT = 0.5
439	_LEASE_TTL = 5.0
440	_LEASE_SID_HEX = 64
441	_LEASE_SEQ_MAX = 20
442	_LEASE_TS_LEN = 16

444	# snapshot. A sidecar is always one or more whole records because it is
445	# published only by a temp-file/rename, so a reader can never see a torn one.
446	_LEASE_REC_LEN = (len(_LEASE_REC_PREFIX) + _LEASE_SEQ_MAX + 1
447	                  + _LEASE_SID_HEX + 1 + _LEASE_TS_LEN + 1)

450	def _iter_snapshot_frames(items):
451	    """Yield the canonical put frames of a committed snapshot, one at a time.
452	
453	    ``items`` must already be sorted by the keys' raw UTF-8 bytes. Each
454	    frame uses the same deterministic framing as the log, so the sequence
455	    is identical on every platform for the same snapshot -- and streaming
456	    it frame by frame never holds the whole image in memory at once.
457	    """
458	    for key, value in items:
459	        yield _encode_frame(_OP_PUT, value, key=key)
460	
461	
462	def _snapshot_image(items) -> bytes:
463	    """Canonical byte image of a committed snapshot: one put frame per key.
464	
465	    The image is the concatenation of :func:`_iter_snapshot_frames` over
466	    the sorted items, identical on every platform for the same snapshot.
467	    """
468	    return b"".join(_iter_snapshot_frames(items))
469	
470	
471	def _snapshot_id(items) -> bytes:
472	    """Content identity of a committed snapshot (32 raw bytes).
473	
474	    Computed incrementally over the canonical image: the hash runs frame
475	    by frame, so deriving an identity never holds the whole image in
476	    memory at once.
477	    """
478	    digest = hashlib.sha256()
479	    for frame in _iter_snapshot_frames(items):
480	        digest.update(frame)
481	    return digest.digest()

484	def _encode_token(seq: int, sid: bytes, lo: bytes | None,
485	                  hi: bytes | None, pos: int) -> bytes:
486	    """Serialise a scan position; the exact inverse of :func:`_decode_token`."""
487	    flags = (1 if lo is not None else 0) | (2 if hi is not None else 0)
488	    parts = [_TOKEN_MAGIC, seq.to_bytes(8, "big"), sid, bytes((flags,))]
489	    for bound in (lo, hi):
490	        raw = bound if bound is not None else b""
491	        parts.append(len(raw).to_bytes(4, "big"))
492	        parts.append(raw)
493	    parts.append(pos.to_bytes(8, "big"))
494	    body = b"".join(parts)
495	    return body + zlib.crc32(body).to_bytes(4, "big")
496

498	def _decode_token(tok: bytes):
499	    """Parse a scan token into ``(seq, sid, lo, hi, pos)``.
500	
501	    Every malformation -- wrong magic, truncation, trailing garbage, a
502	    checksum mismatch, unknown flags, a hidden endpoint or a reversed
503	    range -- raises ``ValueError``; nothing is guessed or repaired.
504	    """
505	    if len(tok) < 4 + 8 + 32 + 1 + 4 + 4 + 8 + 4:
506	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
507	    if tok[:4] != _TOKEN_MAGIC:
508	        raise ValueError("not a scan token")
509	    if int.from_bytes(tok[-4:], "big") != zlib.crc32(tok[:-4]):
510	        raise ValueError("scan token checksum mismatch")
511	    off = 4
512	    seq = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
513	    off += 8
514	    sid = tok[off:off + 32]
515	    off += 32
516	    flags = tok[off]
517	    off += 1
518	    if flags & ~0x03:
519	        raise ValueError("scan token carries unknown flags")
520	    bounds = []
521	    for present in (flags & 1, flags & 2):
522	        if off + 4 > len(tok) - 4:
523	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
524	        size = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 4], "big")
525	        off += 4
526	        if off + size > len(tok) - 4:
527	            raise ValueError("scan token is truncated")
528	        if not present and size != 0:
529	            raise ValueError("scan token carries a hidden endpoint")
530	        bounds.append(tok[off:off + size] if present else None)
531	        off += size
532	    if off + 8 != len(tok) - 4:
533	        raise ValueError("scan token length mismatch")
534	    pos = int.from_bytes(tok[off:off + 8], "big")
535	    lo, hi = bounds
536	    if lo is not None and hi is not None and lo > hi:
537	        raise ValueError("scan token range is reversed")
538	    return seq, sid, lo, hi, pos

541	class _SnapshotBox:
542	    """Strong box around one user's materialised, pinned snapshot.
543	
544	    A box is the unit the reclamation logic counts as a user: every open
545	    cursor and every read-only store holds its own box for the snapshot it
546	    serves. Boxes live in a process-wide :class:`weakref.WeakSet`, so a
547	    cursor or reader that is garbage collected without an explicit
548	    ``close()`` releases its pin automatically -- the in-use table can
549	    neither leak nor outlive the snapshots it protects. The content
550	    identity is hashed lazily, so a scan that neither mints a token nor
551	    registers a cross-process lease pays no hashing cost.
552	    """
553	
554	    __slots__ = ("seq", "items", "_sid", "__weakref__")
555	
556	    def __init__(self, seq, items, sid=None):
557	        self.seq = seq
558	        self.items = items
559	        self._sid = sid
560	
561	    def sid(self) -> bytes:
562	        if self._sid is None:
563	            self._sid = _snapshot_id(self.items)
564	        return self._sid

567	# Process-wide set of snapshots currently in use. Every open cursor and
568	# every live read-only store keeps a box here for its pinned snapshot; the
569	# writer's reclamation never removes the published copy of any snapshot
570	# named in this set. The set is weak, so users closed normally (or simply
571	# dropped) release their pin with no bookkeeping. The boxes also keep the
572	# materialised bytes alive in memory, so a token minted in this process
573	# resolves without touching disk even across stores.
574	_PINS: "weakref.WeakSet" = weakref.WeakSet()
575	
576	
577	def _register_snapshot(seq: int, items, sid=None) -> _SnapshotBox:
578	    """Register one user (a cursor or a reader) pinning a snapshot."""
579	    box = _SnapshotBox(seq, items, sid)
580	    _PINS.add(box)
581	    return box
582

584	def _unpin_snapshot(box: _SnapshotBox) -> None:
585	    """Release the pin held by a closing cursor or reader."""
586	    _PINS.discard(box)

589	def _release_lease(leases, seq: int, sid: bytes) -> None:
590	    """Release a GC'd cursor's cross-process lease; never raises.
591	
592	    A cursor dropped without ``close()`` releases its in-process pin through
593	    the weak pin set; this gives the same treatment to its cross-process
594	    lease so a forgotten cursor cannot pin a copy forever.
595	    """
596	    try:
597	        leases.release(seq, sid)
598	    except Exception:
599	        # Finalizers must never raise into the garbage collector.
600	        pass

603	def _pid_alive(pid: int) -> bool:
604	    """Best-effort liveness check for the process a lease sidecar names.
605	
606	    A lease whose owner process no longer exists expires on the spot --
607	    no heartbeat can ever come from it again -- so the writer treats its
608	    records as stale and sweeps the file without waiting out the TTL. Any
609	    doubt (a process owned by another user, an unsupported platform, a
610	    transient error) reads as *alive*: expiring a live holder's lease would
611	    break its protection, while a dead holder's lease also expires by
612	    heartbeat TTL, only later.
613	    """
614	    if pid == os.getpid():
615	        return True
616	    if sys.platform == "win32":  # pragma: no cover - windows only
617	        return _pid_alive_windows(pid)
618	    try:
619	        os.kill(pid, 0)
620	    except ProcessLookupError:
621	        return False
622	    except OSError:
623	        # PermissionError and friends: the process exists but is not ours
624	        # to signal, which is proof enough of life.
625	        return True
626	    return True
627

629	def _pid_alive_windows(pid: int) -> bool:  # pragma: no cover - windows only
630	    """OpenProcess-based liveness check for Windows.
631	
632	    ``os.kill(pid, 0)`` cannot be used there: any signal value other than
633	    ``CTRL_C_EVENT``/``CTRL_BREAK_EVENT`` terminates the target process.
634	    """
635	    try:
636	        import ctypes
637	        kernel32 = ctypes.windll.kernel32
638	        # PROCESS_QUERY_LIMITED_INFORMATION.
639	        handle = kernel32.OpenProcess(0x1000, False, pid)
640	        if not handle:
641	            return False
642	        try:
643	            code = ctypes.c_ulong()
644	            if not kernel32.GetExitCodeProcess(handle, ctypes.byref(code)):
645	                return True
646	            return code.value == 259  # STILL_ACTIVE
647	        finally:
648	            kernel32.CloseHandle(handle)
649	    except Exception:
650	        return True

653	def _live_snapshot_keys() -> set:
654	    """The ``(seq, sid)`` pairs with at least one user in this process."""
655	    return {(box.seq, box.sid()) for box in _PINS}

658	def _pinned_snapshot(seq: int, sid: bytes):
659	    """Materialised items for a live in-process pin, or ``None``.
660	
661	    The identity is compared only for boxes already on the token's
662	    sequence, so a resolution against an unpinned sequence hashes nothing.
663	    """
664	    for box in _PINS:
665	        if box.seq == seq and box.sid() == sid:
666	            return box.items
667	    return None

670	class _LeaseManager:
671	    """Cross-process registry of snapshots currently in use.
672	
673	    A process that opens a read-only store or holds a cursor or resume
674	    session over some snapshot -- on either open form of the store -- owns
675	    exactly one lease sidecar --
676	    ``wal.lease.<pid>.<rand>``, all of the single ``wal.lease.*`` kind --
677	    listing every snapshot that process has in use, one fixed-width
678	    ``wal.l<seq>.<sid>.<heartbeat>\\n`` record each. The file is rewritten
679	    atomically (temp file, rename; no fsync, because a lease need not
680	    survive a crash) on every change and every heartbeat, so another
681	    process never observes a half-written record: what it reads is one
682	    complete lease image or the previous one.
683	
684	    Because each process writes only its own file, registering, refreshing
685	    and removing a lease never races another process's lease. An orderly
686	    ``close()`` deletes the sidecar; a process killed without closing simply
687	    stops heartbeating. Expiry is then detected two ways: the heartbeat
688	    timestamps go stale after the TTL, and a sidecar whose owning process no
689	    longer exists expires immediately -- a dead owner can never heartbeat
690	    again. The writer reads *all* lease sidecars before reclaiming a copy,
691	    so a snapshot a cursor or a read-only store in any process is serving is
692	    never removed.
693	
694	    A lease is a protection, never a requirement: writes are best-effort, so
695	    a read-only directory simply has no sidecar and reading is unaffected,
696	    while the in-process pins still apply.
697	    """
698	
699	    def __init__(self, directory: str):
700	        self._dir = directory
701	        # A unique name per process instance. The random suffix keeps two
702	        # incarnations of one pid (pid reuse, or processes sharing a copied
703	        # directory) from ever touching one sidecar.
704	        self._name = f"{_LEASE_PREFIX}{os.getpid()}.{uuid.uuid4().hex}"
705	        self._path = os.path.join(directory, self._name)
706	        # Snapshot keys this process currently leases, reference counted: a

1121	def _iter_frames(f):

1123	
1124	    For every intact frame yields
1125	    ``("frame", meta, value, start, end)``. Scanning stops with either no
1126	    terminal event (clean EOF), ``("torn", start)`` for a single incomplete
1127	    final frame, or ``("invalid", start)`` for a frame that fails framing,
1128	    header/payload checksum or metadata parsing. With the header checksum a
1129	    partial header that borrows bytes from a following record cannot survive,
1130	    so a short read landing exactly at EOF is reliably the one unfinished
1131	    record a single writer was appending when it died; bytes left beyond such
1132	    a read instead make it corruption.
1133	    """
1134	    f.seek(0, os.SEEK_END)
1135	    eof = f.tell()
1136	    f.seek(0)
1137	    while True:
1138	        start = f.tell()
1139	        header = f.read(_HEADER)
1140	        if not header:
1141	            return
1142	        if len(header) < _HEADER:
1143	            # Trailing bytes of a frame header are a torn tail only when
1144	            # nothing follows them; a gap anywhere else is corruption.
1145	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
1146	                   else ("invalid", start))
1147	            return
1148	        if header[:4] != _MAGIC:
1149	            yield "invalid", start
1150	            return
1151	        if int.from_bytes(header[_PREFIX:], "big") != zlib.crc32(
1152	                header[:_PREFIX]):
1153	            yield "invalid", start
1154	            return
1155	        length = int.from_bytes(header[4:_PREFIX], "big")
1156	        if length > _MAX_PAYLOAD:
1157	            yield "invalid", start
1158	            return
1159	        payload = f.read(length)
1160	        checksum = f.read(_TRAILER)
1161	        if len(payload) < length or len(checksum) < _TRAILER:
1162	            # Only the single final record may be incomplete.
1163	            yield (("torn", start) if f.tell() == eof
1164	                   else ("invalid", start))
1165	            return
1166	        if int.from_bytes(checksum, "big") != zlib.crc32(payload):
1167	            yield "invalid", start
1168	            return
1169	        newline = payload.find(b"\n")
1170	        if newline < 0:

1172	            return
1173	        try:
1174	            meta = json.loads(payload[:newline])
1175	        except (ValueError, UnicodeDecodeError):
